title: ChatGPT's Meetings plugin reaches Pro and Business users on macOS
subtitle: The DevDay-launched note-taker that listens through the Mac's audio — no bot in the call — is finishing its gradual rollout to all eligible accounts.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI's Meetings plugin, which it introduced at DevDay on September 29, has finished rolling out to all Pro and Business accounts on the ChatGPT macOS desktop app, according to help-center updates and user reports today. The plugin captures a call by listening to the Mac's microphone and system audio and streaming it to OpenAI, then produces a personalized summary with suggested action items. The notes land as a private page inside ChatGPT Space; the raw audio is deleted from the device and OpenAI's servers once the summary is written and cannot be replayed.

The design choice that distinguishes Meetings from the field — Otter, Fireflies, Zoom AI Companion, Microsoft Copilot — is that it does not join the call as a bot participant. There is no icon on the attendee list, no notice to the other participants from the meeting platform, and no reliance on a specific conferencing provider's API. The plugin is as happy with an in-person conversation picked up by the laptop microphone as with a Zoom call piped through Mac system audio. That capability also means the ethical and legal burden sits entirely with the user: single-party consent jurisdictions permit this; two-party consent jurisdictions, which include California and many European countries, require everyone in the conversation to agree.

The rollout is tightly scoped. Enterprise accounts remain in a limited alpha, Windows, iOS, and Android support is listed only as "coming soon," and the macOS build still has limits on meeting length and background processing that enterprise customers typically require. The important question is less about the plugin's features and more about where OpenAI pushes it next: if Meetings becomes a default surface on ChatGPT Enterprise, it competes directly with Microsoft Copilot's meeting features at every joint account the two share. Microsoft has visibility into those calls through Teams; OpenAI has visibility through the macOS client. The data layer those two products build on top of will matter more over time than the feature list.

A takeaway for learners: when a tool is this easy to run without the other participants knowing, the technology question (does it work?) separates fast from the ethics question (should you?). Before you install Meetings on a work laptop, read your employer's recording policy, your jurisdiction's consent law, and the ChatGPT data-use terms. Then decide whether the summary is worth the trust cost. The feature is useful; the habit around it is what you are actually choosing to adopt.
